subject: humanities
passage: Bidriware, a craft of the city of Bidar in southern India, produces vessels and ornaments whose silver patterns gleam against a surface of deep black. The black is not paint. Craftsmen first cast an object in an alloy that is mostly zinc with a little copper, engrave a design into it, and hammer fine silver wire into the grooves. The piece is then rubbed with a paste containing ammonium chloride and soil traditionally dug from within the old fort at Bidar. The paste reacts with the zinc alloy and turns it permanently black, but it leaves the silver untouched, so the inlaid design, until then barely visible, stands out in bright contrast. Why that soil works so well is still debated; artisans insist no substitute gives the same finish.
stem: According to the text, why does the silver design on a piece of Bidriware stand out so clearly?

choices.A: The silver is polished after the paste has darkened the entire surface of the object.
choices.B: The paste blackens the zinc alloy around the silver without changing the silver itself.
choices.C: The engraved grooves are deeper than the silver wire, creating shadows around the design.
choices.D: The paste reacts with the silver and makes it brighter than the surrounding alloy.

explanation.why: The text explains the final step: the paste "reacts with the zinc alloy and turns it permanently black, but it leaves the silver untouched." The contrast comes from the alloy darkening while the silver stays as it was, so the design "stands out in bright contrast."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions polishing, and it says the paste leaves the silver untouched rather than darkening everything.
explanation.B: Correct. The alloy turns black and the silver is "untouched," which is exactly what creates the contrast.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the depth of the grooves or about shadows.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text: the paste reacts with the zinc alloy, not with the silver.
